# Agents and Automated Tools

This document outlines rules and requirements for AI automation agents and automated
tooling that interact with the Node.js project.

Existing Node.js collaborators (as listed in the README.md) may use AI agents to
contribute but must do so responsibly.

New Node.js contributors should avoid using AI agents to interact with the project.

## Code Contributions

* **No unreviewed automation**: Automated pull requests must not be created without
  ongoing human oversight. The pull request must be actively maintained by a human
  contributor who responds to feedback. The AI agent is not permitted to create pull
  requests, open issues, post comments, respond to reviews, or push commits without
  ongoing human oversight.

* **Commit responsibility**: Commits created with agent assistance must follow all
  Node.js [commit message guidelines](./doc/contributing/pull-requests.md#commit-message-guidelines).
  The human contributor opening the PR takes full responsibility for the changes.

* **Testing and verification**: All changes must pass the Node.js continuous integration.
  Human judgment must verify that existing tests are not removed or modified inappropriately,
  and that new tests correctly validate the intended behavior.

### Requirements

* All commits must be signed off by the human user using `Signed-off-by: Your Name <your@email.example>`
  as an attestation to the [Developer Certificate of Origin](https://developercertificate.org/).
* AI-assistance must be acknowledged using the `Assisted-by: <agent name>` annotation.
* AI-authored code contributions must be compatible with the project's licensing and
  contribution guidelines.

## Prohibited Activities

AI agents **must not**:

* Push to any branch or tag in nodejs/node.
* Create unsupervised pull requests or issues without active human engagement.
* Make claims about code without human verification against actual source code.
* Remove or modify existing tests without human judgment.
* Interact with the repository through means other than those explicitly authorized.
* Use commit messages to promote for-profit AI tools or commercial brands. A single
  `Assisted-by: <agent-name>` annotation is required disclosure, not promotion, and is
  permitted.
* Post AI-generated messages directly into pull requests, issues, or project communication
  channels without direct human review and editing to ensure clarity, accuracy, and respect
  for collaborator time.
* Sign off commits using `Signed-off-by: <agent name>` or `Co-authored-by: <agent name>`.

## Violations

Automated interactions that violate these rules may result in:

* Immediate closure of pull requests without review.
* Blocking of the automation tool from further interaction with the project.
* Blocking of the tool's account or its owner from contributing.
* Reports to relevant platforms or organizations operating the automation.

***

For more information on AI use in general contributions (not specific to agents),
see [AI use policy and guidelines](./doc/contributing/ai-guidelines.md).

# Contributing to Node.js

> \[!TIP]
> Contributing for the first time? Please read our
> [Guide for First-Time Contributors](./doc/contributing/first-contributions.md) for tips
> and answers to FAQs.

Contributions to Node.js include code, documentation, answering user questions,
running the project's infrastructure, and advocating for all types of Node.js
users.

The Node.js project welcomes all contributions from anyone willing to work in
good faith with other contributors and the community. No contribution is too
small and all contributions are valued.

The Node.js project has an open governance model.
Individuals making significant and valuable contributions are made
Collaborators and given commit-access to the project. See the
[GOVERNANCE.md](./GOVERNANCE.md) document for more information about how this
works.

Pull Requests are the way concrete changes are made to the code, documentation,
dependencies, and tools contained in the `nodejs/node` repository.
Contributors who are not Collaborators may have no more than 10 pull requests
open at a time.

## Automation and bots

An automation tool or bot that is not managed by the Node.js project
must seek explicit authorization by opening an issue with their owner
in [nodejs/admin](https://github.com/nodejs/admin) before interacting
with the project.

Interactions (including Issues, Comments, Pull Requests and Reviews) made
by an automation that was not authorized by Node.js collaborators are
subject to immediate moderation enforcement on the automation and owner
without notice.

Node.js requires contributors to understand and take full responsibility for
every change they propose. Pull requests containing AI-generated code the
contributor has not personally understood, tested, and verified will likely be closed
without review.

See [details on our AI use policy and guidelines](./doc/contributing/ai-guidelines.md).

## Support

Looking for help? Check out the
[instructions for getting support](.github/SUPPORT.md).

## Release types

* **Current**: Under active development. Code for the Current release is in the
  branch for its major version number (for example,
  [v22.x](https://github.com/nodejs/node/tree/v22.x)). Node.js releases a new
  major version every 6 months, allowing for breaking changes. This happens in
  April and October every year. Releases appearing each October have a support
  life of 8 months. Releases appearing each April convert to LTS (see below)
  each October.
* **LTS**: Releases that receive Long Term Support, with a focus on stability
  and security. Every even-numbered major version will become an LTS release.
  LTS releases receive 12 months of _Active LTS_ support and a further 18 months
  of _Maintenance_. LTS release lines have alphabetically-ordered code names,
  beginning with v4 Argon. There are no breaking changes or feature additions,
  except in some special circumstances.
* **Nightly**: Code from the Current branch built every 24-hours when there are
  changes. Use with caution.

Current and LTS releases follow [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). A
member of the Release Team [signs](#release-keys) each Current and LTS release.
For more information, see the
[Release README](https://github.com/nodejs/Release#readme).

### Download

Binaries, installers, and source tarballs are available at
<https://nodejs.org/en/download/>.

#### Current and LTS releases

<https://nodejs.org/download/release/>

The [latest](https://nodejs.org/download/release/latest/) directory is an
alias for the latest Current release. The latest-_codename_ directory is an
alias for the latest release from an LTS line. For example, the
[latest-hydrogen](https://nodejs.org/download/release/latest-hydrogen/)
directory contains the latest Hydrogen (Node.js 18) release.

#### Nightly releases

<https://nodejs.org/download/nightly/>

Each directory and filename includes the version (e.g., `v22.0.0`),
followed by the UTC date (e.g., `20240424` for April 24, 2024),
and the short commit SHA of the HEAD of the release (e.g., `ddd0a9e494`).
For instance, a full directory name might look like `v22.0.0-nightly20240424ddd0a9e494`.

#### API documentation

Documentation for the latest Current release is at <https://nodejs.org/api/>.
Version-specific documentation is available in each release directory in the
_docs_ subdirectory. Version-specific documentation is also at
<https://nodejs.org/download/docs/>.

### Verifying binaries

Download directories contain a `SHASUMS256.txt.asc` file with SHA checksums for the
files and the releaser PGP signature.

You can get a trusted keyring from nodejs/release-keys, e.g. using `curl`:

```bash
curl -fsLo "/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" "https://github.com/nodejs/release-keys/raw/HEAD/gpg/pubring.kbx"
```

Alternatively, you can import the releaser keys in your default keyring, see
[Release keys](#release-keys) for commands on how to do that.

Then, you can verify the files you've downloaded locally
(if you're using your default keyring, pass `--keyring="${GNUPGHOME:-~/.gnupg}/pubring.kbx"`):

```bash
curl -fsO "https://nodejs.org/dist/${VERSION}/SHASUMS256.txt.asc" \
&& gpgv --keyring="/path/to/nodejs-keyring.kbx" --output SHASUMS256.txt < SHASUMS256.txt.asc \
&& shasum --check SHASUMS256.txt --ignore-missing
```

report.overview: This is the Node.js runtime itself at v26.10.0 — a C++/V8 host (src/, ~495 files) wrapping a JavaScript standard library (lib/, ~429 files) that is compiled into a V8 startup snapshot at build time. Beyond upstream-familiar surface, this tree carries several large experimental subsystems wired through the same plumbing: a `node:vfs` virtual file system that intercepts `node:fs` and the module loaders at reserved mount points under `os.devNull/vfs/<id>`, a `node:ffi` libffi-backed foreign function interface gated by a `kFFI` permission scope, a `node:dtls` endpoint/session stack, a `node --experimental-bench` benchmark runner mirroring the test runner, and a vendored Rust crate set (`deps/crates`, temporal_rs + ICU) linked as a staticlib. The audience is Node core collaborators; the distinctive engineering property is that every new capability is a triple — a CLI option in `src/node_options.cc`, a `setupX()` in `pre_execution.js` that calls `BuiltinModule.allowRequireByUsers()`, and an internal binding registered in `src/node_binding.h`.

system_map.summary: Execution begins in `src/node_main.cc` (`main`/`wmain`) which calls `node::Start`, which after SEA argv fixup loads the V8 startup snapshot and runs a `NodeMainInstance`. C++ then picks exactly one main script from `lib/internal/main/` via a linear dispatch in `src/node.cc`; that script calls into `lib/internal/process/pre_execution.js` to configure the realm before user code. The JS layer talks to C++ only through `internalBinding()`, whose registry is the `NODE_BUILTIN_*_BINDINGS` macro list in `src/node_binding.h`. Build is GYP/Make (`configure.py` → `node.gyp` → `Makefile`) with a secondary GN path, plus Cargo for `deps/crates`. There is no deployment target in the usual sense: the artifact is the `node` binary, optionally repackaged as a single executable application by `src/node_sea.cc`.

claims.claim: The process entrypoint is `main()` (POSIX) / `wmain()` (Windows, which UTF-8-converts wide argv and refuses pre-Windows-10 unless `NODE_SKIP_PLATFORM_CHECK=1`), both delegating to `node::Start`.

`node::Start` first runs `sea::FixupArgsForSEA` so a single-executable build can rewrite its own argv, then calls `StartInternal`, which branches to `sea::BuildSingleExecutable`/`WriteSingleExecutableBlob` or `GenerateAndWriteSnapshotData` before falling through to `LoadSnapshotData` + `NodeMainInstance::Run`.

C++ selects the JS main script by an ordered if-chain in `src/node.cc`: worker_thread → inspect → print_help → prof_process → eval_string → check_syntax → bench_runner → test_runner → watch_mode → run_main_module → repl → eval_stdin. Adding a new run mode means adding a branch here plus a file in `lib/internal/main/`.

The JS↔C++ boundary is the `internalBinding()` registry declared by macro lists in `src/node_binding.h`; optional subsystems are compiled in conditionally — `quic` behind `HAVE_OPENSSL && OPENSSL_NO_QUIC != 1`, `dtls` behind `HAVE_OPENSSL && HAVE_DTLS`, `sqlite`/`webstorage` behind `HAVE_SQLITE`, `ffi` behind `HAVE_FFI`.

`lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js` is executed by `Realm::BootstrapRealm()` and is normally *not* run at startup — its resulting V8 heap is captured into the build-time snapshot by `SnapshotBuilder::Generate()`; `--no-node-snapshot` forces real execution. It must stay synchronous and must not read argv or env at top level.

`prepareExecution()` in `pre_execution.js` is the single funnel every main script passes through; it patches the process object, runs ~25 `setupX()` initializers, calls `initializePermission()`, initializes the module loaders, and mounts the VFS before returning the resolved main entry.

The storage layer is threefold: the real file system via the `fs`/`fs_dir`/`glob` bindings, SQLite via `src/node_sqlite.cc` (which now exposes virtual tables through a `VirtualTableModule` wrapping `sqlite3_module`), and Web Storage via the `webstorage` binding gated on `--experimental-webstorage`.

External native dependencies are vendored under `deps/` (v8, uv, openssl, ada, llhttp, nghttp2, ngtcp2, simdjson, sqlite, undici, zlib, zstd, libffi, LIEF, perfetto, postject) rather than fetched, so builds are hermetic.

`deps/crates` is a Rust staticlib (`crate-type = ["staticlib"]`, `node_crates` v14.6.202, rust-version 1.86) vendoring `temporal_rs`/`temporal_capi` and the ICU4X crates; its Cargo.toml is generated by node-core-utils and must not be hand-edited.

Build/test commands: `./configure && make -j4`, `make test` (tooltest + addon builds + cctest + jstest), `make test-only` (skips doc build), `make test-ci` for CI, `make lint` (js/cpp/md/yaml), `make coverage`.

`configure.py` owns feature toggles that become gyp variables — `--shared-ffi`/`--without-ffi` set `node_use_ffi`, and `--v8-enable-temporal-support` gates the Rust temporal path; `node.gyp` defaults `node_use_ffi%` to `false` and only pulls in `deps/libffi/libffi.gyp:libffi` when it is true.

Type checking of `lib/` is opt-in and non-emitting: `tsconfig.json` sets `allowJs: true`, `checkJs: false`, `noEmit: true`, excludes `src`/`tools`, and maps every public builtin id to its `lib/*.js` file plus `internal/*` to `lib/internal/*`.

Hand-written ambient types for the C++ boundary live in `typings/internalBinding/*.d.ts` (one file per binding, including `ffi.d.ts`), loaded via `tsconfig.json`'s `files` list alongside `typings/globals.d.ts` and `typings/primordials.d.ts`.

Python tooling is linted by ruff configured in `pyproject.toml` with deliberately huge thresholds (`max-complexity = 100`, `max-statements = 289`, `line-length = 172`), reflecting long-lived legacy scripts like `configure.py` (112 KB) and `tools/test.py`.

feature_catalog.summary: User-facing surface is the CLI plus the `node:*` builtin module set. The CLI's 'subcommands' are really the run-mode branches in `src/node.cc` — `node inspect`, `node --test`, `node --experimental-bench`, `node --watch`, `node -e`, `node --check`, `node --prof-process`, `node --build-snapshot`, `node --build-sea`, and the default script/REPL/stdin paths. Module features are individually flag-gated and only become requirable when a `setupX()` in `pre_execution.js` calls `BuiltinModule.allowRequireByUsers()`. This tree's notable additions over a stock runtime are `node:vfs`, `node:ffi`, `node:dtls`, `node:bench`, `node:quic`, `node:sqlite` with virtual tables, and `stream/iter`/`zlib/iter`.

claims.claim: `node:vfs` exposes `create()`, `registerProvider()`, and the classes `VirtualFileSystem`, `VirtualProvider`, `MemoryProvider`, `RealFSProvider`, `ZipProvider`; it is `node:`-scheme-only and requires `--experimental-vfs`.

`--vfs-mount <src>` (repeatable) and `--vfs-load <src>` both append to the same `vfs_mounts` option vector; `--vfs-load` additionally sets the `[vfs_load_set]` implied bool so the entry point can be taken from inside a mount.

`node:ffi` provides `DynamicLibrary` plus typed pointer accessors (`getInt8`…`getFloat64`, `setInt8`…, `exportBytes`, `getRawPointer`, `kFastArguments`) and emits an experimental warning at module load.

`node:bench` mirrors the test runner's API shape — `bench`, `suite`/`describe`, `before`/`after`/`beforeEach`/`afterEach`, `run`, `runFile`, `createRunner` — and is reached from the CLI by `node --experimental-bench`, which routes to `internal/main/bench_runner`.

`node:dtls` exposes `connect`, `listen`, `createSecureContext`, and `DTLSEndpoint`/`DTLSSecureContext`/`DTLSSession`, backed by `src/dtls/{dtls,dtls_context,dtls_endpoint,dtls_session}.cc`; `DTLSEndpoint` manages a UDP socket and routes datagrams to sessions.
The permission model (`--permission`) exposes `process.permission.has()` / `.drop()` and nine scopes: fs (with read/write children), child, wasi, worker, inspector, net, addon, ffi, openssl.store.
`--permission-audit` is a distinct mode from `--permission`: `isAuditMode()` reads it separately and `Permission::EnableWarningOnly()` makes denials warn rather than throw.

Single-executable applications are configured by a JSON file parsed in `src/node_sea.cc` supporting `useSnapshot`, `useCodeCache`, `assets`, and `disableExperimentalSEAWarning`; assets are serialized into the blob and read back as `string_view` pairs.

SEA assets can be surfaced as a read-only mounted VFS via `initSeaVfs()`, which places the SEA main script at the mount-point root so `__dirname`-relative `require()` calls inside a bundled app resolve to bundled assets.

`node --watch` is implemented as a supervisor process: `internal/main/watch_mode.js` strips watch flags into `argsWithoutWatchOptions`, re-`spawn`s `process.execPath`, and drives restarts from a `FilesWatcher` with a 200 ms debounce in `filter` or `all` mode.

The test runner CLI parses options via `parseCommandLine()`, supports `--test-isolation=none` (which defers user-module loading into `run()`), forces concurrency 1 when the inspector is active, and sets a nonzero exit code from the `test:summary` event.
`--experimental-stream-iter` unlocks two additional builtins in one shot, `stream/iter` and `zlib/iter`, via the same `allowRequireByUsers` mechanism.

`node:sqlite` is enabled by default (disabled only by `--no-experimental-sqlite`) and now supports user-defined virtual tables: `VirtualTableModule` populates an `sqlite3_module` with `xCreate`/`xConnect`/`xBestIndex`/`xOpen`/`xClose` trampolines.

Documented public API pages exist for every new subsystem — `doc/api/vfs.md`, `ffi.md`, `dtls.md`, `bench.md`, `quic.md`, `stream_iter.md` — so a feature is not considered landed without its doc page.

data_flow.summary: Input boundaries are argv/env (parsed into `EnvironmentOptions` by `src/node_options.cc` and read from JS via `getOptionValue()`), the file system, sockets, and the SEA blob embedded in the binary. Options are the master state: essentially every JS feature branch keys off `getOptionValue('--flag')`, and options are re-read after deserialization by `refreshRuntimeOptions()`. The heaviest transform in this tree is the VFS path router, which reroutes `node:fs` calls and module-loader fs calls whose resolved path falls under a reserved mount prefix, before those calls reach the native `fs` binding. State owners are the `Environment` object on the C++ side and, on the JS side, module-level singletons: `vfsState.handlers` in `internal/fs/utils.js`, the `loaderOverrides` map in `internal/modules/helpers.js`, the `providers` array in `provider_registry.js`, and `Module._cache`/`_pathCache` in the CJS loader.

claims.claim: CLI/NODE_OPTIONS parsing populates `EnvironmentOptions` fields declared in `src/node_options.h` (`vfs_mounts`, `experimental_vfs`, `vfs_load`, `allow_fs_vfs`) which JS then reads through `internal/options`'s `getOptionValue()`.
`refreshRuntimeOptions()` is the first call inside `prepareExecution()`, re-reading options after snapshot deserialization so a snapshotted heap does not carry stale build-time option values.

Every VFS mount is assigned a numeric layer id and is served at `${os.devNull}/vfs/<id>`; because `os.devNull` is a character device (`/dev/null`, `\\.\NUL`) it can have no children, so path ownership is decidable from the string alone without touching the disk.

`getLayerIdFromPath()` parses the layer id with a hand-rolled digit scan over char codes 47/92 (`/`, `\`) rather than splitting — a deliberate hot-path optimisation since it runs on candidate fs calls.

Dispatch into the VFS is a single null-check per fs function: `lib/fs.js` reads `vfsState.handlers` and, if non-null, calls the handler and routes the returned promise through `vfsResult()`/`vfsVoid()` to the error-first callback; when no VFS is mounted the field is `null` and overhead is one comparison.
`setVfsHandlers()` is the only writer of `vfsState.handlers` and is imported by `internal/vfs/setup.js`, making that file the single install point for fs interception.

Module resolution is redirected separately from `fs`: `internal/modules/helpers.js` wraps each native loader method and consults a `loaderOverrides` map installed by `setLoaderOverrides()`, with a `hasLoaderOverrides` boolean short-circuit when the map is empty.

`internal/modules/run_main.js` deliberately calls loader methods through `loaderMethods` rather than the `modules` binding directly, precisely so a mounted VFS can override them and a worker entry point can live inside one.

Unmounting must invalidate loader state: `cleanForVfsPrefix()` walks `Module._cache`, `Module._pathCache`, `statCache`, `realpathCache`, and the package.json caches, deleting entries under a mount prefix — by value for `_pathCache`, whose keys are `request\0parent` tokens.

The provider selection pipeline is source-sniffing, not extension-based: `canHandle()` for `zip` attempts `ZipFile.openSync()` (which locates the end-of-central-directory record) and stashes the opened archive in `pendingZipFile` so `create()` does not reopen it; `dir` falls back to `stats.isDirectory()`.

Permission denials feed a diagnostics channel: `Permission::is_scope_granted` calls `Publish()` on failure, which emits `{scope, resource, dropped}` on a per-scope channel and guards against recursion with a `publishing_` flag so a subscriber's own checks cannot re-enter.

`normalizeReference()` in the JS permission layer canonicalises input across three representations — `URL` (converted with `fileURLToPath` only for `fs.*` scopes), `Uint8Array` (passed through raw so non-UTF-8 paths are not mangled), and validated strings.

SEA data flows binary→memory: `WriteSingleExecutableBlob` serialises the asset map with a length-prefixed count, and the reader rebuilds an `unordered_map<string_view, string_view>` pointing into the still-mapped blob rather than copying.

Worker threads receive their entry through the message port (`LOAD_SCRIPT` in `internal/worker/io`), not argv, and call `finishVfsMounts()` themselves so mounts are re-created per thread rather than shared.

behavior_traces.summary: Three flows characterise the runtime: cold startup of a script, mounting a VFS and loading an entry point from inside it, and a permission-checked FFI `dlopen`. All three share the same spine — C++ picks a main script, that script calls `prepareExecution()`, and `prepareExecution()` decides what the realm is allowed to do. The VFS trace is the most intricate because mounting is deliberately deferred past `--import` preloads so a preload can register a custom provider. The FFI trace is the clearest example of a two-check security path, where a purely in-memory operation still demands filesystem-write permission for platform-consistency reasons.

claims.claim: Cold start (script): `main()` → `node::Start` → `sea::FixupArgsForSEA` → `StartInternal` → `LoadSnapshotData` → `NodeMainInstance::Run` → C++ `StartExecution` picks `internal/main/run_main_module`.

`run_main_module.js` then calls `prepareMainThreadExecution(!isEntryURL)` → `markBootstrapComplete()` → `RegExpPrototypeExec(/^/, '')` to reset RegExp statics before user code → `Module.runMain(mainEntry)`.

`Module.runMain` is invoked even for ESM entry points solely to preserve legacy monkey-patchability of `Module.runMain` by `--require` preloads; the file comments this as undesirable and slated for removal once module customization hooks suffice.

Inside `prepareExecution()` the order is fixed: `refreshRuntimeOptions()` → `patchProcessObject()` → trace/inspector/navigator/warning setup → the feature `setupX()` block → `initializeReport()` → `setupDiagnosticsChannel()` → `initializePermission()` → source maps → deprecations → `setupVmModules()` → `initializeModuleLoaders()` → `finishVfsMounts()` → `setupHttpProxy()`.

Each flag-gated builtin is unlocked by the same three lines — check `getOptionValue('--experimental-X')`, require `BuiltinModule` from `internal/bootstrap/realm`, call `allowRequireByUsers('X')` — repeated verbatim in `setupBench`, `setupFFI`, `setupSQLite`, `setupStreamIter`, `setupDTLS`, `setupQuic`, `setupVfs`.

VFS mount trace: `finishVfsMounts()` guards on `vfsMounted` → reads `--vfs-mount` entries → `path.resolve` + `fs.statSync` each (throwing `ERR_VFS_INVALID_TARGET` on failure or on a non-file/non-dir) → `selectProvider()` → `new VirtualFileSystem(provider)` → `vfs.mount()`.

Mounting is called from two places with an idempotence guard: from `prepareExecution()` only when `--import` is empty, otherwise from `run_main` after the `--import` loop — so an `--import` preload can `registerProvider()` before any source's provider is chosen.

For `--vfs-load`, `getVfsLoadIndex()` re-walks `process.execArgv`-style option names to recover which position in the shared `vfs_mounts` list came from `--vfs-load`, because the option parser stores plain strings and cannot record provenance.

The `--vfs-load` source is spliced into `process.argv` at index 1 rather than overwriting it, so the program's own first positional argument is not silently dropped; `argv[1]` names the real source while the reserved mount point stays an implementation detail.
`src/node.cc` routes to `run_main_module` when `vfs_load` is set even with no positional argument, instead of falling through to the REPL or stdin-eval — a dedicated branch added for this flag.

FFI trace: `new ffi.DynamicLibrary(path)` → `DynamicLibrary::New` → construct-call check → `THROW_IF_INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS(kFFI)` → null-byte check on the path → optional byte materialisation → `uv_dlopen` → `image.AfterOpen()`.

When an FFI library is supplied as bytes (a library living inside a VFS that `dlopen` cannot reach by path), the code additionally demands `kFileSystemWrite` on `AddonImage::TempDir()` — and comments that the check is enforced even on Linux where an anonymous memfd is used, so grants do not vary by platform.

`initializePermission()` hardens the realm before granting: it replaces `process.binding` with a thrower, `ObjectFreeze`s the `path` module so it cannot be monkey-patched to defeat path checks, emits `SecurityWarning` codes PERM0001–PERM0007 for each dangerous `--allow-*`, and only then defines `process.permission`.
Without `--permission`, passing any `--allow-*` flag is a hard error: the else-branch iterates `availableFlags()` and throws `ERR_MISSING_OPTION`, preventing a false sense of restriction.

Worker startup diverges: `internal/main/worker_thread.js` calls `prepareWorkerThreadExecution()` (which asserts `initializeModules === false`), waits for a `LOAD_SCRIPT` message on the env message port, and only then calls `initializeModuleLoaders` and `finishVfsMounts`.

testing_signals.summary: Testing is dominated by the bespoke Python harness `tools/test.py`, which discovers suites under `test/<suite>/`, applies per-suite `.status` files for SKIP/SLOW/FLAKY expectations, and shells out to the built `node` binary per test file. There is no Vitest/Jest; the stack tag is misleading. Native code is covered by `cctest` (googletest) and the `js-native-api`/`node-api`/`addons` suites, which require a build step before they can run. Coverage is collected by nyc/c8 with `.nycrc` thresholds of 95% lines/statements and 93% branches, uploaded to Codecov from two Linux workflows. The new subsystems are well covered at the JS level — ~121 `test-vfs-*` files in `test/parallel` alone plus a dedicated `test/ffi/` suite — but SEA-specific paths are explicitly excluded from coverage.

claims.claim: The harness is `tools/test.py`, a Python 3 runner invoked as `./tools/test.py --flaky-tests keep_retrying -p actions -j 4`; suites are directories under `test/` and each may carry a `<section>.status` file read by `ReadConfigurationInto`.

risk_map.summary: The highest-value security surfaces are the permission model, `node:ffi`, and the VFS path router — and they interact. FFI is a documented memory-unsafe API whose only guard is the `kFFI` scope; the VFS is documented as explicitly *not* a security boundary despite superficially resembling a sandbox; and the permission model's correctness depends on non-obvious hardening (freezing `path`, killing `process.binding`) that a refactor could silently undo. Fragile coupling concentrates in the VFS's reliance on string-prefix path ownership and on cache invalidation across five separate module-loader caches. The `--vfs-load` provenance recovery by re-parsing execArgv is the most brittle single mechanism in the tree.

claims.claim: `node:ffi` is memory-unsafe by design — the docs state that invalid pointers, wrong signatures, or use-after-free 'can crash the process or corrupt memory' — and its only gate is `THROW_IF_INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS(kFFI)`, which is a no-op unless `--permission` is on.

`--allow-ffi` is only offered in `availableFlags()` when `--experimental-ffi` is set, so the flag surface changes shape depending on another flag; a script probing `availableFlags()` for capability discovery can get inconsistent answers.

The VFS is documented as NOT a sandbox: 'The VFS API is not a sandbox, permission system, or access-control mechanism', and `RealFSProvider`'s root-escape rejection is explicitly stated not to be a security boundary. Any code treating a mount as isolation is wrong.

VFS path ownership is decided purely by string prefix against `${os.devNull}/vfs`; the safety argument rests on `os.devNull` being a character device that cannot have children. A platform where that assumption fails, or a `path.resolve` normalisation difference, would break routing exactness.

`getVfsLoadIndex()` recovers which mount came from `--vfs-load` by re-walking argument names and counting `--vfs-mount`/`--vfs-load` occurrences, including manual handling of the space-separated `--vfs-mount value` form. Any change to option parsing or aliasing silently misattributes the entry point.

Unmount correctness depends on `cleanForVfsPrefix()` clearing five distinct caches (`Module._cache`, `Module._pathCache` by value, `statCache`, `realpathCache`, package.json caches); missing one leaves resolvable stale entries pointing into an unmounted layer.

The permission model's integrity relies on two side effects that look like incidental hardening: replacing `process.binding` with a thrower and `ObjectFreeze(require('path'))`. Removing either reopens a documented bypass.

`Permission::Publish` guards re-entrancy with a mutable `publishing_` flag rather than a scope guard; an exception thrown from a diagnostics-channel subscriber would leave `publishing_` stuck true and silently suppress all further permission telemetry.

Zip provider detection performs a trial `ZipFile.openSync()` inside `canHandle()` and caches the handle in module-level `pendingZipFile`; if a later provider's `canHandle` throws or `create()` is never reached, that file handle leaks and a subsequent probe reuses stale state.

`registerProvider()` unshifts onto a module-global array with no removal API and no ordering control beyond 'newest wins', and the doc comment confirms a registered provider 'can back, wrap, or vet any source' — a `--require`/`--import` preload can therefore intercept every subsequent mount.

`node --watch` shells out: it `spawn`s `process.execPath` with reconstructed argv and manipulates `NODE_OPTIONS`, making it a command-construction path where flag stripping bugs change what the child is allowed to do (a recent commit addressed exactly this: 'watch: strip watch flags from NODE_OPTIONS in child process').

`src/node_file.cc` is the largest source file (5851 lines) and contains ~55 `THROW_IF_INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS` call sites; each new fs syscall wrapper is an opportunity to omit one, and there is no compile-time enforcement that a binding method performs its check.

Blast radius: `lib/internal/process/pre_execution.js` is on the critical path of every execution mode (main thread, worker, shadow realm, test runner, bench runner), so a fault in any `setupX()` breaks all entry points at once.

`--vfs-load` is force-disabled for workers by mutating `per_isolate_opts->per_env->vfs_load = false` in `src/node_worker.cc`; this cross-layer write means main-thread and worker option state intentionally diverge, which is easy to overlook when reasoning about option values in JS.

SEA construction writes an executable to disk from a JSON config with `assets` and `useSnapshot`/`useCodeCache`, and `FixupArgsForSEA` rewrites argv before any option parsing — a supply-chain-relevant path where the config file fully determines the resulting binary's behaviour.

extension_points.summary: This codebase is unusually explicit about where new code plugs in, because adding a feature is a repeated four-part ritual. New native capability goes in the `NODE_BUILTIN_*_BINDINGS` macro lists; new CLI surface goes in `src/node_options.cc` with a field in `node_options.h`; new run modes go in the `StartExecution` if-chain plus a file in `lib/internal/main/`; new user-visible builtins are gated by a `setupX()` in `pre_execution.js` calling `BuiltinModule.allowRequireByUsers()`. Beyond core, the VFS provider registry, the CJS `Module._extensions` table, the loader-override map, and the SQLite virtual-table module are genuine runtime plugin surfaces.

claims.claim: `BuiltinModule.allowRequireByUsers(id)` is the runtime gate that makes a `lib/*.js` module requirable by user code; it adds to `canBeRequiredByUsersList` and conditionally to `canBeRequiredByUsersWithoutSchemeList` (new experimental modules are added `node:`-scheme-only).

`vfs.registerProvider({ name, canHandle, create })` is the public plugin interface for `--vfs-mount` sources; registrations are unshifted ahead of the built-in `zip` and `dir` providers, so a custom provider outranks both.

`VirtualProvider` in `lib/internal/vfs/provider.js` is the base class a custom provider subclasses; the shipped implementations (`MemoryProvider`, `RealFSProvider`, `ZipProvider`, and the internal SEA provider) are the reference shapes.

`setLoaderOverrides(overrides)` installs per-key replacements for the module loader's fs and package.json operations; passing a nullish field restores the native fast path, which is how unmount cheaply reverts loader interception.

`Module._extensions` is the classic CJS extension table (`.js`, `.json`, `.node` assigned in `cjs/loader.js`) and `findLongestRegisteredExtension` supports multi-dot extensions, so a loader plugin can register e.g. `.test.ts`.

`Module._load`, `Module._resolveFilename`, and `Module._findPath` remain intentionally monkey-patchable — `resolveMainPath()` comments that `Module._findPath` 'is monkey-patchable here', and the repo's own `eslint.config.mjs` patches `Module._resolveFilename` to resolve vendored ESLint plugins.

Adding a native binding means adding `V(name)` to the appropriate macro list in `src/node_binding.h` — `NODE_BUILTIN_STANDARD_BINDINGS` for unconditional ones, or a new `#if`-guarded `NODE_BUILTIN_X_BINDINGS(V)` block for optional subsystems.

Adding a CLI flag is a paired edit: `AddOption("--flag", help, BOOL_FIELD(field), kAllowedInEnvvar-style)` in `src/node_options.cc` and the field declaration in `src/node_options.h`; `Implies()` links derived bools (as `--vfs-load` implies `[vfs_load_set]`).

Adding an execution mode requires a branch in the `StartExecution` chain in `src/node.cc` and a corresponding script in `lib/internal/main/`; `bench_runner` is the most recent instance of this pattern and mirrors `test_runner` line for line.

`sqlite.createModule()` backed by `VirtualTableModule` lets user JS supply `xBestIndex`/`xOpen`/`xClose` behaviour into SQLite's `sqlite3_module` vtable — a genuine C++-level plugin surface reachable from JS.

Permission scopes are extended by adding a `V(Name, "dotted.name", Parent, "--allow-flag")` entry to the `PERMISSIONS(V)` macro in `permission_base.h`; the enum, the diagnostics channel names, and the string mapping are all generated from it.
Test suites are pluggable: each `test/<suite>/` may carry a `testcfg.py` and a `<suite>.status` file that `tools/test.py` discovers, as `test/ffi/` does.

Lint is composed from per-directory partial configs (`lib/eslint.config_partial.mjs`, `test/`, `doc/`, `benchmark/`, `tools/eslint/`) assembled by the root `eslint.config.mjs`, plus a custom `tools/eslint-rules` plugin directory — the place to add core-specific rules.

The internal binding type surface is extended by adding a `typings/internalBinding/<name>.d.ts` file; recent commits ('typings: wire up quic internal binding types', 'typings: add mksnapshot internal binding types') show this is expected alongside the C++ change.

agent_handoff.summary: Read `AGENTS.md` first — it is binding policy, not advice, and it forbids an agent from pushing, opening PRs, or posting comments without active human oversight. Code style in `lib/` is not ordinary JavaScript: everything goes through `primordials` to be immune to user monkey-patching, and a custom ESLint plugin enforces it. Before editing, understand that `lib/` is snapshotted at build time, so top-level side effects in bootstrap files have outsized consequences. Nothing in `deps/` should be hand-edited. The realistic verification loop is a full build followed by targeted `tools/test.py` runs, not a fast unit-test cycle.

claims.claim: `AGENTS.md` requires `Signed-off-by:` from the human contributor and an `Assisted-by: <agent name>` annotation, and explicitly prohibits `Signed-off-by:`/`Co-authored-by:` naming an agent, pushing to any branch or tag, and creating unsupervised PRs or issues.

Read these first, in order: `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `doc/contributing/primordials.md`, `doc/contributing/cpp-style-guide.md`, and `lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js` (whose header comment is the best single explanation of startup ordering).

Every file in `lib/` destructures from `primordials` at the top (`ArrayPrototypePush`, `StringPrototypeStartsWith`, `ObjectFreeze`, …) instead of using built-in methods directly; new code must match this or `tools/eslint-rules` will reject it.

Never hand-edit `deps/`: `deps/crates/Cargo.toml` states 'This manifest is generated by node-core-utils. Do not modify it directly', and dependency bumps are driven by `tools/dep_updaters/` and scheduled workflows.

Anything added to `lib/internal/bootstrap/` must be synchronous and must not read argv or env at top level, because it is executed at snapshot-build time; runtime-dependent setup belongs in `pre_execution.js` or a `lib/internal/main/` script.

Verification loop: `./configure && make -j<n>` then `python3 tools/test.py parallel/test-<pattern>` for targeted runs; full validation is `make test-only` (build addons + cctest + jstest + tooltest without rebuilding docs).

Lint before proposing a change: `make lint` runs js/cpp/md/yaml; `make lint-ci` adds Python lint and a merge-conflict-marker scan across `benchmark deps doc lib src test tools` that fails the build on stray `<<<<<<<`/`>>>>>>>`.

Safe edit boundary: a feature that is JS-only (a new provider, a runner reporter, a stream helper) can be added without touching C++. Anything needing a new syscall, a new option, or a new permission scope requires coordinated edits across `src/node_options.{cc,h}`, `src/node_binding.h`, and `pre_execution.js`.

Trap: options are read twice — once at parse time into `EnvironmentOptions` and again in JS via `getOptionValue()` after `refreshRuntimeOptions()`. Caching an option value at JS module scope before that call yields a stale snapshot-time value.
Trap: `permission.js` memoizes `_permission`, `_audit`, and `_ffi` on first read, so an option consulted before `refreshRuntimeOptions()` is frozen for the process lifetime.

Trap: worker option state is not the main thread's — `src/node_worker.cc` overwrites `vfs_load` to false per worker, so a JS-side `getOptionValue('--vfs-load')` reasoning must account for thread identity.

Trap: `test/ffi`, `test/sqlite`, `test/addons`, `test/js-native-api`, and `test/node-api` all need a build step (`make build-ffi-tests`, etc.) before `tools/test.py` will pass on them; failures there on a fresh tree usually mean 'not built', not 'broken'.
CI asserts the tree is unchanged after tests run, so any test that writes into the repo (rather than a tmpdir) will fail the Linux workflow even if the assertions pass.

Use `test/common/index.js` capability predicates (`hasFFI`, `hasDtls`, `hasQuic`, `hasSQLite`, `hasTemporal`, `hasCrypto`) to guard new tests for conditionally-compiled features rather than assuming a full-featured build.
Public API changes are incomplete without the matching `doc/api/*.md` page and YAML metadata block (`added: vX.Y.Z`, `Stability: 1 - Experimental`), as every subsystem in this tree carries one.

You are working in the Node.js runtime source tree (v26.10.0, branch `main`, remote https://github.com/nodejs/node.git). This is not an application — it is a C++/V8 host plus a JavaScript standard library, and the build artifact is the `node` binary itself.

SHAPE. `src/` (~495 files) is the C++ host; `lib/` (~429 files) is the JS standard library; `deps/` vendors every native dependency (v8, uv, openssl, libffi, sqlite, undici, simdjson, plus `deps/crates`, a Rust staticlib carrying temporal_rs and ICU4X); `test/` holds ~863 suite files driven by a bespoke Python harness; `tools/` holds build, lint, and doc tooling; `doc/api/` holds the public API reference.

C++ then picks exactly one main script via a linear if-chain in `src/node.cc` (~L351-413): worker_thread, inspect, print_help, prof_process, eval_string, check_syntax, bench_runner, test_runner, watch_mode, run_main_module, repl, eval_stdin. That script calls `prepareExecution()` in `lib/internal/process/pre_execution.js`, which is the single funnel for every execution mode. `lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js` is normally NOT executed at runtime — its heap is captured into the V8 startup snapshot at build time, so it must stay synchronous and must not read argv or env at top level.

DISTINCTIVE SUBSYSTEMS. Beyond the familiar builtins, this tree carries `node:vfs` (a virtual file system that intercepts `node:fs` and the module loaders at reserved mount points under `${os.devNull}/vfs/<id>`, with a pluggable provider registry), `node:ffi` (libffi-backed, memory-unsafe, gated by a `kFFI` permission scope), `node:dtls`, `node:bench` (a benchmark runner mirroring the test runner's API), `node:quic`, and SQLite virtual tables.

THE FOUR-PART RITUAL. Adding a user-visible capability almost always means four coordinated edits: (1) `AddOption(...)` in `src/node_options.cc` plus a field in `src/node_options.h`; (2) a `V(name)` entry in a `NODE_BUILTIN_*_BINDINGS` macro in `src/node_binding.h` if native code is involved; (3) a `setupX()` in `pre_execution.js` that checks `getOptionValue('--experimental-X')` and calls `BuiltinModule.allowRequireByUsers('x')`; (4) a `doc/api/x.md` page with a YAML `added:` block. New run modes additionally need a branch in `src/node.cc` and a file in `lib/internal/main/`.

CONVENTIONS. All of `lib/` uses `primordials` (`ArrayPrototypePush`, `StringPrototypeStartsWith`, …) instead of built-in methods, so user monkey-patching cannot subvert internals; a custom ESLint plugin in `tools/eslint-rules` enforces this. Never hand-edit `deps/` — those are updated by `tools/dep_updaters/` and scheduled workflows. `typings/internalBinding/*.d.ts` carries hand-written types for the C++ boundary.

CI also asserts the working tree is unchanged after tests run, so tests must write only to tmpdirs.

Options are read twice (parse time, then JS after `refreshRuntimeOptions()`); `internal/process/permission.js` memoizes its option reads permanently. `src/node_worker.cc` force-disables `vfs_load` per worker, so main-thread and worker option state intentionally diverge. The VFS is explicitly documented as NOT a security boundary.
